title: Iran’s oil leverage is weakening. That could push it toward escalation | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

Iran’shold over the Strait of Hormuz is slipping,and experts warn that a cornered Tehran has tended to choose escalation over capitulation.

Oil isflowing againdespite continued Iranian attacks on shipping in the waterway, eroding the leverage Tehran has wielded against the United States since the war began. Now, Iran may be looking for ways to break the stalemate as US President Donald Trump piles economic pressure on the Islamic Republic in the hope of forcing it to make concessions.

Iran rattled the global energy marketat the outset of the conflictwhen it effectively shuttered the maritime chokepoint through which a fifth of the world’s oil passed before the war. The price of oil surged globally, prompting some economists to warn of a worldwide recession should the closure continue.

American consumerswere dealt higher pricesat the gas pump, and spiraling energy costs were seen as a major factor in big Republican losses in the US midterm election this month. Trump himself acknowledged that the war was partly to blame for his party’s defeat.

But a global recession never materialized. Oil exports from the region are now close to pre-war levels, and the global market may soon have more crude than it needs. For Iran, that’s a problem.

Iranian officials have nonetheless claimed victory, arguing that Tehran’s closure of the strait has already yielded major strategic gains.Mohsen Rezaei,head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, made his country’s intention clear: “We want to impose a cost on the Americans that makes attacking Iran too expensive, and that serves as a deterrent.”

Experts say one of Iran’s main wartime strategies – exerting pressure on global energy markets – may now be losing its potency.

Danny Citrinowicz, a senior fellow at the Institute for National Security Studies in Israel, said that Tehran has long sought to “internationalize” the cost of war. But “if oil prices continue to fall despite Iranian attacks, an important part of that strategy becomes less effective,” he told CNN.

Oil prices have fallen sharply in recent weeks despite an escalation in Iranian attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

TheInternational Energy Agencyattributes this to recovered Gulf exports, with oil supply expected to surpass demand in the fourth quarter for the first time since the outbreak of the Iran war in February.

“It certainly seems that Iran is either unwilling or unable to prevent the flow of crude oil at present,” David Oxley, chief climate and commodities economist at the consultancy firm Capital Economics, told CNN, adding that “navigability in the strait is still far short of pre-crisis norms.”

Ahria Roushanbakhti, head of the fuel desk at Axis Limited, the Middle East’s largest energy liquidity provider, said that while Iran may be losing some of its hold on the waterway, its ability to cause significant damage to energy infrastructure in the region remains worrying.

Iran experts say that at this point in the conflict, Tehran is unlikely to dampen its demands but rather escalate its military operations to break the “neither war nor peace” stalemate with the US that is crippling Iran’s economy.

Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, said that Tehran appears more confident than ever after Trump’s midterm setback, celebrating the Republican Party’s losses.

But oil prices dipped after the midterm results as fears eased that Trump would reignite the war and Tehran ramped up diplomacy with mediators.

“Markets appear to be increasingly assuming that a return to full-scale war is unlikely and that oil supplies will gradually recover,” Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group (ICG) think tank, told CNN.

“But that assumption could change quickly if Iran decides to intensify the confrontation,” he said.

That may be unfolding, as Iran already appears to be looking at other options to pressure the US back to the negotiating table.

Added threats by the US may even force Iran into more proactive measures that would be costly for both sides, experts said.

The conflict has escalated rapidly in recent days after a period of relative calm. The region saw a series of back-and-forth attacks by Iran and allied Houthi rebels in Yemen on Gulf countries, as well as US attacks on Iranian territory around the strait.

Presented with the possibility of perceived capitulation or military escalation, Iran’s hardline regime has tended to choose the latter despite the cost, experts say.

“When it feels cornered, it may become more aggressive, not less,” Citrinowicz said.

Iran may choose to increase pressure on tankers using the US-supported route in the Strait of Hormuz, said Azizi, of the International Crisis Group. It may also choose to disrupt ship-to-ship transfers of oil, or target Gulf infrastructure or alternative export routes that allow Gulf countries to bypass some Tehran’s restrictions in Hormuz, he said.

Tehran also appears to be lowering the threshold for retaliation. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) on Tuesday said it targeted American radars in Bahrain following unspecified “US drone violations of Iran’s airspace.” It has also warned Bahrain’s Sunni rulers against mistreatment of the majority Shiite population.

Iran has warned countries against allowing the US to use their territory to attack it. National security chief Rezaei said last week that “all military bases… from Western Asia to Europe, will be legitimate targets.”

“There will be no safe distance or safe haven for aggressors,” he warned, adding that “no base will remain immune.”

This shows that Iran may not only be looking to expand its scope of operations, but is now “signaling that even violations of its airspace could trigger attacks against American assets,” Azizi said.

Others believe there is not much else the Islamic Republic can do that can bring Washington to agree to a deal that works for Iran.

Parsi of the Quincy Institute said that further action by Iran will not make a difference. What could make a change, he said, is the one thing that Iranians are disinclined to do: give Trump a “symbolic” victory that is “ego-soothing and face-saving.”

The Iranians, he said, are more opposed to a symbolic loss than a substantive one, which only adds to the stalemate.

Meanwhile, a third US aircraft carrier strike group recently entered US Central Command’s area of responsibility, where it is expected to – at least temporarily – join ongoing operations that include enforcing a blockade of Iranian ports and escorting commercial ships willing to transit the strait.

Washington may be misjudging Iran’s breaking point, experts said.

Tehran’s latest operations fit into a “broader shift in Iranian military thinking toward more proactive deterrence,” Azizi said.

“If the leadership concludes that its leverage over Hormuz is weakening while the American blockade continues to impose economic costs, it may decide to go further, potentially even challenging US naval forces more directly,” he said.

This would be considerably riskier, he said “but Iran may see it as necessary to break the blockade rather than allow its position to deteriorate gradually.”
